name: Lime Requirement Calculator
seoDesc: Lime raises soil pH, and the amount needed depends on how far the pH must rise and how heavy the soil is. Free lime requirement calculator: enter your values
summary:
Lime raises soil pH, and the amount needed depends on how far the pH must rise and how heavy the soil is. It returns lime required, as pure CaCO₃ equivalent, application splits recommended and pH increase per tonne, and the panel shows all of them at once.

This calculator estimates the rate from a target pH and a buffer index, and warns when the change is large enough to split over seasons. Every result is derived from the boxes you fill in, so changing one input updates the whole panel at once. Units are stated on every box and in every result, so a figure copied out of a protocol, a datasheet or a chart can be entered without converting it first.

sections.title: The formula behind the Lime Requirement
sections.html:
Lime (t/ha) ≈ (target pH − current pH) × buffer factor × texture factor

The symbols in the formula
SymbolWhat it stands forUnit
ΔpHchange in pH requiredpH units
bufferbuffer index from a soil test—
texturetexture factor, 1.0 for sand down to 0.18 for clay—

sections.title: How do I use the Lime Requirement?
sections.html:
The form asks only for what the formula needs — nothing is optional decoration.

  1. Enter the values you already have. Every box accepts a decimal point and a minus sign; thousands separators are ignored.
  2. The grey boxes are results: they are worked out from your inputs and cannot be typed into.
  3. Press Calculate. The results fill in together, and from then on they follow every edit you make — there is no page to reload and nothing to submit.

sections.title: A worked example
sections.html:
Take the default values the page opens with: current ph of 5.4, target ph of 6.5, soil texture set to Loam, buffer index of 6.4.

Substituting them into the formula gives lime required of 2.82 t/ha, as pure caco₃ equivalent of 2.53 t/ha, application splits recommended of 2, ph increase per tonne of 0.3906.

The arithmetic is the page's own: change one box and the result moves by the amount the formula implies, which is the quickest way to convince yourself the tool is honest.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
• Clay soils need more lime per unit of pH because they have far more exchange sites to neutralise.

  • Lime moves slowly — about 2.5 cm a year in the profile — so a large requirement is split over two or three seasons rather than applied at once.

  • Use a buffer index test where available; the texture factor alone is a rough estimate.

sections.title: What are the common mistakes?
sections.html:
The arithmetic is simple; the inputs are where things go wrong. The usual culprits:

  • Applying the full rate when the requirement exceeds 4–5 t/ha.
  • Lime and ammonium fertilizer applied in the same operation, which loses nitrogen as ammonia.
  • Chasing a high pH where the crop prefers acid soil — blueberries at pH 7 will be chlorotic.

faq.q: How much does pH rise per tonne of lime?
faq.a: About 0.1–0.3 pH units on a loam; much more on sand, much less on clay.
Dolomitic lime does; calcitic lime does not, so check the soil test for magnesium.

faq.q: What does the Lime Requirement actually calculate?
faq.a: It returns lime required, as pure CaCO₃ equivalent, application splits recommended and pH increase per tonne. Each one is derived by the formula on this page, so you can check any figure by hand.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — and if you change an input, every result updates with it.

faq.q: Why is the answer different from the one in my protocol?
faq.a: Nearly always a unit or a rounding difference. This calculator works in the units printed next to each box, keeps full precision internally and only rounds for display, so recomputing from the rounded numbers on screen can differ in the last digit.

faq.q: Can I use it with the numbers straight from a datasheet?
faq.a: Yes. Every box states its unit, and nothing is converted behind your back, so a figure copied from a datasheet, a kit insert or a protocol goes in as printed.
